 The tightening in some time spreads and firming in physical premiums that have 
accompanied the sharp decline in base metals prices reflect the continued 
improvement in the fundamental picture. It is ironic that the market’s attention has 
shifted away from physical indicators just when they are looking the strongest they 
have been in some time. In particular, demand concerns for some metals seem 
excessive, with global aluminium demand running at record high, and copper and 
nickel demand only marginally below their historical peaks. 
 In our view, China has hit a pivot point. With copper supply chain inventory fully 
destocked, participants are now drawing on SHFE and bonded stocks. Even scrap is 
tighter. As our focus section analyses, we believe scrap usage is being maximised 
and do not believe it will offer a reprieve from a supply-constrained market. 
 We remain bullish on copper prices in H2, but we have marked to market our price 
forecasts lower, taking the annual average down 9%, to $10,412/t. For the same 
reason, we have also lowered our price expectations for the other base metals, apart 
from aluminium. Given booming and broad-based global demand, we now see price 
strength continuing through H2 and have raised our forecast higher to reflect this.  
 Precious metals prices have come under pressure as the dollar has strengthened, 
concerns over a slowdown have materialised, and successive increases in margin 
requirements have weighed upon silver. In our view, silver prices have lacked 
fundamental support in the last leg higher; thus, they are likely to remain volatile 
until they find support from physical demand, which we expect to materialise 
around the low 30s, support or retail demand returns to the driving seat.

FOCUS: UNTANGLING THE SCRAP DIMENSION TO BASE METALS IN 2011 
Scrapping our way to the truth 
 
The scrap market is a significant component in fundamental dynamics for base metals. 
In this focus piece, we consider the effect of scrap market fundamentals on the copper 
and aluminium markets in 2011 and beyond. 
 
Given mine supply tightness, scrap will be key for growth in refined copper output this 
year. We believe that the strong price signal, growing industrial activity and continued 
improvement in emerging market scrap supply chains will lead to further growth in 
global scrap supply this year.  
 
But the degree of copper scrap supply improvement will be constrained by limitations on 
old scrap supply, with little latent material to use. We believe that scrap usage is already 
being maximised through the copper supply chain, but do not believe that this will offer 
a sudden reprieve from a supply-constrained market. 
 
In a tight primary aluminium market, exacerbated by financing deals, scrap demand has 
risen. However, beyond short-term factors such as the effect of the Japan earthquake on 
autos, we see no reason to believe that scrap supply should improve enough in 2011 to 
plug the gap. The key remains an increase in obsolete scrap supply in China to a level of 
equilibrium with demand growth from semis, and that remains some years off, with the 
scrap market remaining tight in the interim. 
A search on Metal Bulletin reveals more than 50 stories this year alone about metal thefts, 
the BBC has also reported a number of stories on the topic and just last week, Reuters 
reported that British Railways cable thefts had jumped 67% this year. The increased 
occurrences of metal thefts illustrate the high value being placed on scrap metal and the 
strong demand for it. Scrap forms an important part of the copper and aluminium markets, 
yet it is all too often overlooked, mainly because it is an incredibly opaque industry about 
which is very difficult to obtain information. Nevertheless, the ebb and flow of scrap 
availability has important implications for the refined copper and primary aluminium 
markets, accounting for more than a third of the copper industry and more than a quarter 
of the aluminium industry. In this month’s focus, we analyse the methods by which scrap 
penetrates the copper and aluminium markets, changes in scrap usage trends and the 
outlook for scrap supply and its implications for refined and primary metals markets.  
Scrap plays a volatile role in the copper market  
In the copper market, scrap enters the system through two routes: production (through its 
use in the refining process) and consumption (through its use in semi-fabricated products). 
This means that scrap can be a competitor with concentrate (in the production process) 
and refined metal (through consumption).  
Scrap use in refined output is more fluid and volatile than in consumption (semis) because 
there is more flexibility in the production process of the former. The amount of scrap that 
can be used in the production of refined copper is, in theory, almost limitless, bound only by 
availability and/or the technology in use. It is for this reason that there is such a big 
difference in the proportion of secondary in refined between countries. In Germany, for 
instance, the ratio is as high as almost 60%, while in the US it is 3% because the gradual 
decline in the manufacturing base and cheaper scrap processing costs in China have 
resulted in a large portion of US scrap now being exported for processing elsewhere. The

large manufacturing base of Germany generates a large volume of scrap, so the domestic 
industry has been structured to maximise this through having dedicated secondary smelters 
and through refineries having the technological capability to use large volumes of scrap. 
Illustrating the flexibility in this area of scrap use is the change in proportion of secondary 
used in refined output over the past two decades. This figure rose from just over 14% in the 
mid-1980s to almost 18% by the mid-1990s, falling to a low of 12% in 2003 before rising to 
a record high of over 19% in late 2010. The two key factors behind the changes in scrap use 
in refined output are supply and price, which we will discuss in the next section. 
Over the past decade, the trend has been a steady increase in the proportion of secondary 
used in refined output. Indeed, it has been the stronger growth in both secondary refined 
output and SXEW cathode production that has been responsible for much of the growth in 
refined output in recent years, with primary copper output constrained by tight concentrate 
availability. Although SXEW cathode output and secondary refined output are still far 
smaller contributors to total refined output (accounting for about 35%) than primary 
(which accounts for 65%). The single most important factor behind the increase in global 
secondary refined output is increase industrial activity resulting in a steady increase in scrap 
generation. The source of this has predominantly been the industrialisation of the emerging 
markets, in particular China. Chinese secondary refined output has grown 17% over the 
past decade, while for the world ex-China, this has actually declined slightly. This is largely a 
function of the flow of scrap into China, with the explosion of low-cost Chinese secondary 
facilities attracting large import volumes of historically low copper content scrap. Indeed, 
outside China, secondary as a share of refined has actually fallen from 13% to 11%, while in 
China it has risen from 26% to 38% over the past decade. The jump in Chinese scrap 
imports has played a key role in raising its share of secondary refined output, though 
increased domestic scrap generation has played a part. Like Germany’s, China’s smelters 
have increasingly positioned themselves to be able to process the scrap generated by the 
country’s large domestic manufacturing sector.

In contrast, the ability of consumers to use scrap very much depends on what product they 
produce. For some products, such as wire rod, scrap content needs to be kept at low levels 
(about 5%) while in others, such as low grade bars or profiles, it can be as much as 80%. 
Over the past decade, global direct scrap consumption by consumers is estimated to have 
been 15-30%, with availability being the key determinant of the mix between cathode and 
secondary. Over the past decade, when there has been a sharp contraction in 
manufacturing activity, 2001-02 and late 2008-09, scrap formed a much smaller portion of 
consumer’s raw material mix. We believe this will have recovered above 20% this year. 
Scrap supply is a function of manufacturing activity and price

refined production and consumption (semis production) and the types of scrap used in each 
process. For instance, the generation of new scrap from manufacturing activity (such as run-

typically consumed at the consumer level, while old “life cycle” scrap (from torn down 
buildings, old electronics and white goods and autos) and imports are typically used in 
secondary refined output. The supply of “old” life cycle scrap is largely a function of price, 
whilst the supply of “new” clean post-consumer scrap is largely a function of industrial 
activity. In secondary refined production, the use of scrap is directly a function of availability. 
This is because in secondary refined output, there are lower metallurgical barriers and in 
theory an almost limitless amount of scrap that can be used, which is not the case in semis 
production. So the more scrap there is around, the more scrap will be used in secondary 
refined output. When industrial output is strong, and scrap generation is therefore high, more 
scrap is typically used in refined output, while in periods of recession, low manufacturing and 
lower prices, there is less secondary in refined production.  
However, there is also an indirect relationship with price. That is because the availability of this 
scrap will depend on the level of industrial activity (cars being scrapped and old buildings being 
torn down) and price. When prices are rising, it creates more of an incentive to recover old 
scrap, so an environment of rising or high prices will encourage more old scrap into the system. 
Indeed, this has been the pattern for some years, as rising copper prices have squeezed most of 
the latent scrap out of the system. This source of scrap supply is tied to the life cycle of goods 
and therefore the volume of old scrap that can be tapped into, for any given price, is 
constrained by the level of consumption in the past. For instance, the amount of automotive 
scrap available now will be largely determined by the size of the automotive market 15 years 
ago. Therefore, regardless of price, there are limitations on the potential growth in supply of old 
scrap. Exacerbating this is the trend over recent years of sustained high prices squeezing out all 
latent scrap from the system, leaving very little untapped sources of old scrap.  
How much could scrap use increase? 
A conventional copper smelter will typically have a maximum scrap usage of 15-20%, 
although depending on the number of scrap smelters and the availability of scrap, this number 
can rise significantly. In Germany, where there is a large and established scrap processing 
industry and dedicated scrap smelters, the ratio of secondary refined production is as high as 
60%. This illustrates how much propensity there is to raise scrap in refined output. But the 
major obstacle to growing this figure is the pace and scale of current growth relative to past 
consumption. The rise of emerging market demand means that current consumption rates 
have moved up exponentially, so for some time yet, we believe that the global pool of old 
scrap will be insufficient to allow any significant increases in total scrap use.

In consumption (semis production), however, there are metallurgical barriers to scrap use 
and added complications with using scrap over refined metal. For instance, scrap often has 
extra impurities that have negative environmental effects in burning. Handling it can also be 
difficult. Scrap can be difficult to load efficiently, raising the risk of disruptions or slowing 
down processing. Therefore, its use in semis is more than just a simple function of supply. It 
is also a function of price spreads. Because of quality issues, semi-fabricators will tend to 
prefer to use refined copper as opposed to scrap. However, in an environment where scrap 
discounts are wide, there is a bigger price incentive to maximise scrap usage. When 
discounts are small, fabricators will again increase the proportion of refined metal used in 
their raw material mix because the smaller discount is not enough to outweigh the added 
complexities of using more scrap. For instance, scrap introduces impurities into the furnace 
that would degrade the refractory and the brick lining.  
Scrap in the emerging markets 
There is often the misconception that recycling rates in China are low. In fact, the complete 
opposite is true. As with many emerging markets, the scarcity in raw materials in China has 
forced the country to be an extremely efficient recycler with very high recovery rates, 
especially given that lower labour and unit costs mean that even poor grades of scrap are 
processed. The block in the pipeline is in distribution networks. The small scale of the 
processors and the inefficient cross-provincial networks mean that the industry is often 
clunky and inefficient. However, the Chinese government is rapidly addressing this; in the 
12th five-year plan, the government aims to consolidate the industry and make it more 
efficient by eliminating small scale recyclers. Even though China is an efficient recycler, it 
still has a huge “scrap gap” because of its early stage of economic development. This means 
that there is only a tiny pool of domestic life cycle scrap that it can tap. Consequently, it has 
become a large importer of scrap, with 65% of global imports going there. Large imports of 
old scrap have been key to assisting China’s growth in refined output, given its small 
domestic resource of mined copper relative to metal demand. These imports have played a 
big role in raising China’s secondary refined production to 38% of total refined output from 
26% a decade ago. Scrap imports have been encouraged by a favourable rebate system, 
whereby they used to obtain a 50% VAT rebate, the aim of which was to bring more 
regulation onto the industry to move it from the unofficial economy. However, the 
elimination of this rebate in January 2011 has effectively has raised the cost of scrap relative 
to cathode and could subsequently result in a sharp slowdown in scrap imports, particularly 
if discounts to cathodes narrow.

Scrap supply in 2011 and beyond 
In the copper market, where growth in raw material supply from mines continues to 
stagnate scrap supply and the ability to grow scrap supply is a key factor for the refined 
market balance and prices, we believe that copper mine output will be largely flat this year, 
indeed with the risk skewed to a potential decline. This means that the growth in refined 
output will have to come from scrap. Is this possible, given the already large rebound in 
scrap supply in 2010? Certainly, the incentive has never been as strong. The difficulty in 
sourcing concentrate and the poor outlook for mine supply, together with high prices, are 
creating an environment conducive to maximising scrap use throughout the entire market 
chain. We believe that the strong price signal, growing industrial activity and continued 
improvement in emerging market scrap supply chains will lead to further growth in global 
scrap supply this year and beyond, though the scale of the increase will be constrained. Old 
scrap supply is tied to the life cycle of goods, which means that the volume of old scrap that 
can be tapped into, for any given price, is constrained by the level of consumption in the 
past. Therefore, regardless of price, there are limitations on the potential growth in supply of 
old scrap. Certainly, as China continues to mature, the volume of old scrap that can be 
tapped will steadily, increase though we believe that the growth in current consumption will 
far outpace the growth in old scrap for some time yet. Incentive schemes such as Cash for 
Clunkers that encourage the trading in of old products, eg, autos and consumer goods, for 
discounts on new ones, do provide a temporary boost to old scrap supply, though only by 
bringing it forward. We believe that scrap usage is already being maximised through the 
copper supply chain, but given the limitations outlined above, we do not believe that this 
will offer a sudden reprieve from a supply constrained market. Indeed, in our forecast 
market balance we already forecast scrap growth usage in 2011 (for fabricators, smelter 
and refiners) of close to 20% y/y.

Placing scrap in the aluminium market balance 
While the copper scrap picture has received heightened attention recently due to extreme 
raw material constraints, we believe the aluminium scrap market also requires close 
attention in 2011. The spot primary aluminium market has also begun this year in tight 
fashion. Following a negligible market surplus of 150Kt in 2010 (representing just 0.3% of 
global consumption), in the first quarter of 2011, the global market balance slipped into 
marginal deficit. Exacerbated by warehouse financing deals, primary spot physical market 
conditions have evolved in a direction of tightness. Physical premiums in Europe and the US 
Midwest have soared to multi-year highs, with reports of waiting times of over six months 
to withdraw material from some warehouses in the US. The question, therefore, is whether 
the aluminium scrap supply can potentially moderate the tightness in the spot primary 
market and, hence, premiums, or alternatively, offer another dimension of tightness in the 
overall aluminium market picture in 2011? 
In our view, the answer is in the negative. While higher LME aluminium prices and rising semis 
output (as a function of generally robust levels of industrial production) present a picture of 
rising post-industrial scrap supply, that in itself is likely to have a zero sum effect on scrap 
market balance, given this is driven by an equivalent increase in demand from semis for scrap 
as an input. Post-consumer (or obsolete scrap) supply remains a key variable. However, given 
there are no major scrap incentive programmes in the US or Europe this year (such as Cash for 
Clunkers in 2010) and in China current demand far exceeds growth in scrap from 
obsolescence goods, this is unlikely to offer an escape valve in 2011. The repercussions of the 
natural disaster in Japan via the auto sector may temporarily moderate demand for some 
forms of aluminium scrap, although the broader picture suggests a continued tight balance 
and essentially no bail-out for the spot primary market.   
Aluminium scrap demand likely to rise 
Given its opaque nature, quantifying the exact features of the scrap market remains a 
challenge. Broadly speaking, data suggest that over the past decade, scrap has represented 
20-30% of total global aluminium consumption. Based on the somewhat crude differential 
between semis output (fabrication stage in the aluminium supply chain) and primary 
consumption, data imply that in 2000, scrap usage made up close to 29% of total

does, however, conceal significant regional variations that are important to appreciate. 
Using the same methodology, over the past decade scrap usage as a proportion of total 
demand has averaged 33% in the US, 41% in Germany, 45% in Japan and perhaps most 
significantly only 18% in China (although this masks a rise from just 10% in 2000 to 26% in 
2010). The key point, hence, is that scrap represents close to a quarter of the aluminium 
market and, thus, offers potentially significant fundamental influence.  
To examine the market dynamics for 2011 closer, it is important to have some understanding 
of the structure of the scrap market, linkage to the primary market and longer-term trends in 
usage and generation. Scrap demand of the proportion quoted is generated from semis 
producers, which can be characterised as fabricators producing foundry (diecasters), sheet 
(rolling mills) and extrusions (extruders), sourcing either primary aluminium or scrap to create 
their products. Scrap is sourced by either remelters or secondary smelters, who produce 
casthouse aluminium products that, to an extent, compete with alloy ingot produced by 
primary smelters. Due to the alloyed nature of scrap, remelters and secondary smelters 
produce only alloys. The degree to which these compete with primary aluminium depends 
largely on the type of fabricators product. Diecasting is a form of semis production 
predominantly based on scrap, making up close to 95% of total aluminium used by the sector, 
and this is the case in both the West and China. In terms of milling and extrusions, the picture 
of scrap use is far more constrained, with the West and Brazil using 35-75% of scrap in some 
applications of extruders. In China, this figure falls to closer to 20%.  
There is certainly flex in the system to use higher amounts of scrap, undoubtedly so in 
China, but also in the West in some product areas. In the can sheet/packaging sector, body 
sheets are already pushing 90% scrap usage, so feasibly cannot go any higher. However, 
while extrusions use on average 40% of scrap, some producers have recently trialed an 
extruded billet out of 100% scrap for green building certification, but the market remains 
embryonic. There are limiting factors in some product areas, due to the finishing 
characteristics, where too high a proportion of scrap means it is difficult to anodize or 
results in a different appearance to virgin aluminium. Overall, the market continues to push 
the upper limit wherever it is economically valuable to do so – this is certainly the case in 
Europe, the US and Brazil.

Obsolescence the key to future scrap supply 
The supply picture of the aluminium scrap market can, as with copper, essentially be divided 
into two segments; new scrap generated during the initial manufacturing process (post-
industrial), which is recycled in situ or sent to remelters/secondary smelters, or old scrap, 
which is collected after consumer use has run its course (post-consumer). In terms of a 
distribution between new and old scrap, global data are sparse, but in the US in 2010, the 
USGS reported the ratio at 59:41, while the EAA reported that for Europe in 2008 at 63:32. In 
China, while no figures exist, new scrap is the overwhelming dominant source of supply, given 
the small pool of old scrap due to lower past consumption levels. From a post-industrial 
perspective, the recovery loop is essentially efficient, with no significant regional variations 
(including China), and is unlikely to offer any significant shift in influence on scrap supply in 
the near term. Volumes change with the levels of semis output, but given geographically 
consistent levels of efficiency (hence, little flex for improvement) and a direct correlation to 
rising demand from semis for scrap, it is not a key differentiating fundamental factor. 
Post-consumer scrap generation is, however, a far more significant variable supply influence 
on the scrap market balance. Old scrap comes from the key aluminium consuming end-
product sectors. A recent European Commission (EC) report stated that on a global scale, 
the breakdown of old scrap supply can be given as the transportation sector providing 44%, 
the packaging sector 28%, cable & wire combined with electronics 21%, and the 
construction and building sector 7%. The rate of reclamation within each sector depends 
largely on its scrap processing technology and societal commitment to the collection 
process. The transport sector is the largest supplier of old aluminium scrap and has a high 
reclamation rate, with EC data stating the end of life vehicle rate of collection is 85% in the 
US, Europe and Japan. Over the past decade, however, the transport sector has been a 
source of growing tightness for scrap, primarily due to two factors. First, the rising level of 
aluminium in vehicles has offered an increasing source of demand. For example, in the 
1990s, the average North American vehicle contained 75Kg of aluminium, versus 150Kg in 
2009. Second, given that the average lifetime of vehicles is 12-15 years, the higher 
aluminium content vehicles will not start reaching the end of the life span until the mid-
2010s at the earliest; hence, in the meantime, it provides a deficit drag on the system. 
Incentive programmes such as Cash for Clunkers in the US may encourage early end of life 
decision-making, but such policies are not a feature of the market in 2011. 
The sectors where potential old scrap supply is most likely to improve in the medium term 
are packaging and electronics. In the former (which provides 28% of old scrap), recycling 
rates vary considerably across the globe, with the average rate of 36% masking 
performance from as low as 25% to as high as 85%. These variations are most visible in the 
used beverage can sector, where some nations such as Brazil (97%) and Japan (91%) 
achieve far higher collection rates than other regions such as the US (54%) and Europe 
(63%). Higher rates are largely achieved as a function of the incentive and accessibility 
mechanisms of the collection process. Given there is growing emphasis on greener policies 
by both US and European governments, it is likely that over time the laggards will improve 
rates and, hence, boost supply from this source. The electronics sector is also likely to offer 
an improved source of scrap. Based on EAA figures in 2009, the average European produces 
close to 20Kg of metal old scrap from electronic goods (anything from washing machines 
to TVs), with aluminium representing close to 5% of that. Given that scrap generation from 
this source is expected grow at up to 5% each year, with an ever more intensive use of 
electronic goods, combined with ever shorter life cycles (typically 2-5 years but now 
increasingly shortening), electronics should increase its proportion of total old scrap supply.

China the key to future supply improvement 
Ultimately, though, the key question with regards to old scrap supply is more geographical 
that sectoral. As the world’s largest producer and consumer of aluminium, China is the 
crucial fundamental factor in the primary aluminium balance. Its scrap sector is very much a 
laggard in comparison. Indeed, broadly speaking, it is close to 20 years behind the West in 
terms of usage in the sheet mill and extrusions sectors, with only diecasting operating at a 
similar level of input. Overall scrap use registered at close to 26% in 2010, which offers a 
steady improvement from just 10% a decade earlier but still lags the rest of the world. It is, 
however, the supply side that is most critical, given that in China old scrap generation has 
barely to register as a supply variable.  
So far in China, the pace of obsolete scrap generation has been low; hence, the dependence on 
primary supply has remained well established. In some respects, this is confusing, given the size 
of the Chinese economy and robust levels of growth witnessed over the past decade – surely 
scrap should be plentiful? However, it is the recent nature of this growth story which means 
that old scrap generation has been constrained. Essentially, there is very little old ‘stuff’ in China. 
Sectors such as autos or electronic appliances have increased their output levels at an 
exponential rate over the past few years. For example, motor vehicle production has increased 
from 1.8mn units in 1999 to close to 14mn units in 2009, while air conditioners have increased 
from 13mn units to 81mn units over the same period. The point is that China has yet to reach 
the stage where old scrap generation has reached anywhere near an equilibrium with demand 
for goods containing aluminium. This situation is unlikely to change over the next 5-10 years 
until cars/appliances start coming out of service, having originated from the sharp pickup in 
output in the 2000s. In the mean time, with obsolescence remaining low, the consumption of 
primary will have to remain high. That is not to say there is not the will in China to change the 
significance of the scrap sector – as with copper, the latest 12th Five-Year plan placed greater 
emphasis on recycling with the likely introduction of more recycling plants, which should spur 
greater usage, but this will take time to have a significant effect.

 Following robust gains through April, aluminium prices 
softened early in May, although at close to $2700/t, 
remain firmly in positive year-to-date territory. The 
underlying fundamental trend is firmly supportive, and we 
believe upward price momentum is justified. The 
aluminium physical market remains tightly balanced, 
particularly in the US and Europe, where robust demand, 
combined with the prevalence of financing deals, has led 
to intense competition for material. The Chinese domestic 
market is also healthy with apparent consumption of 
primary aluminium in March rising 10% from the seasonal 
slowdown in February. The only weak note for China has 
come from the growing discount of SHFE to LME prices in 
April. Ongoing support remains from rising energy costs 
and the view that this will inevitably contribute to rising 
production costs. Given a smaller forecast surplus (161Kt), 
owing, primarily, to the strength of demand-side 
performance, we have subsequently upgraded our price 
forecasts with a 2011 average now of $2,620/t. 
 Offering some potential upside risk to prices have been 
official statements from China’s NDRC that it is expecting 
"fairly large" power shortages in the east, north and south 
of the country this summer. In the past when China has 
experienced power shortages, aluminium smelters have 
been among the first and worst affected. This leads us to 
believe that despite China having clear excess aluminium 
smelting capacity, its ability to utilise that capacity fully is 
going to be severely restricted in 2011. If large-scale power 
curbs to smelters are of the scale of H2 10 (June to 
November output fell 2.8Mty), the picture could turn 
extremely bullish.

from physical indicators just when they are looking the

Nickel has endured another month of volatile trading,
ultimately dropping close to $25,000/t, the lowest level
since January this year. Fundamental trends stand in
opposition to this move, and we expect a rebound in
prices. Sustained declines in LME stock levels (down 20Kt 
ytd) are in line with our forecast 30Kt deficit for H1.
Looking towards fundamental conditions in H2 11
though, the potential for a resurgence beyond earlier price
highs lacks immediate justification, in our view. Seasonally 
softer stainless demand during the mid-year period 
combined with ongoing ramp-ups at Barro Alto and Onca
Puma mines, as well as the recovery from disruptions at
Copper Cliff, Harinoche and Cerro Matoso smelters (50Kt
lost output in H1), will marginally soften fundamentals.
However, the forecast market surplus during H2 is a paltry
7Kty, leaving the balance vulnerable to a move into deficit
from supply disruptions. 
 
Despite an upward revision to the Chinese nickel pig iron
output estimate (200Kt in 2011), Chinese refined nickel 
demand has also been stronger than anticipated (+10% 
y/y in Q1). That both are compatible is a function of the
overwhelming strength of stainless output in the country,
which at 3Mt in Q1 is 26% higher y/y and is projected to
reach 3.3Mt in the strong Q2 period (+7% y/y). As a
result, we expect refined nickel imports and production to
remain robust Q2, which is supported by the healthy
premium of domestic Chinese prices versus LME in April.
Moreover, there are risks to NPI output if power rationing
is seriously undertaken in the summer, as Chinese
authorities have indicated. The sustained strength of
Chinese refined nickel demand in spite of rising NPI output
is clearly bullish for the nickel market.

 Tin prices have fallen over the past month, breaking below 
the $30,000/t level for the first time since mid-March this 
year. Such softness is fundamentally justified; the tin 
market has been in a moderate surplus since the beginning 
of year, as reflected in the fact that LME stocks have risen 
30% YTD. Amidst a period of macro headwinds, prices are 
unlikely to gain upward traction until more positive 
fundamental indications emerge. The key factor underlying 
the surplus in 2011 so far has been a sustained destocking 
cycle by smelters in China. Robust domestic refined output 
(+13% y/y in Q1), weak refined imports (-52% y/y in Q1),
and the ongoing discount of Chinese prices to LME, all 
point to an oversupplied domestic market. This has been 
reinforced by the ITRI statement that China has exported 
7-8Kt of refined tin since September last year, making it a 
clear net exporter during the period. This exported material 
was excluded from headline customs figures as it was in 
anode/product form, and only captured in other countries 
import data. Until smelters have fully destocked this 
negative influence on the global balance is unlikely abate. 
 Beyond China, the fundamental picture remains relatively 
healthy and given that Chinese exports have outweighed 
LME stock growth, actually point toward a mild deficit in 
place for the ROW currently which ties in with robust 
physical premia seen in Rotterdam. Indonesian exports 
rose 13% y/y in Q1 11 despite poor weather conditions, 
although recent statements from major producers such 
Timah (whose refined production fell 10% y/y in Q1) 
indicate a more constrained output improvement for 2011 
as a whole. Elsewhere, the ITRI report that smelters are 
avoiding DRC casserite in anticipation of new US supply-
chain regulations, which will place additional pressure on 
an already tight mine supply picture.

 The fundamental picture for zinc is extremely weak, with 
the market still in surplus and the scale of the surplus 
forecast to continue growing over the coming months. 
Zinc’s surplus has been clearly evidenced by the relentless 
rise in SHFE and LME inventories, with the former hitting 
yet new record highs. The stock overhang is now as large 
as it has been since the mid-1990s, which has weighed on 
prices, and we expect this to continue. With mine output 
rebounding and several mines set to ramp up output 
further this year, we see little to constrain the pace of 
refined output growth in the near term. One possible 
short-term risk to this view is Chinese power shortages. 
Guangdong, Jiangxi, Chongqing and Hunan provinces have 
all announced power rationing, which poses the risk of 
production disruptions over the summer. Hunan province, 
for instance, accounts for 18% of Chinese refined zinc 
output, though there have been no reported disruptions so 
far. Given the level of China’s inventory, we believe power 
curbs would have to be more severe than they have been 
in the past for it to tighten the market materially.  
 In terms of demand, a combination of financing deals reducing 
the volume of zinc available for spot delivery and a seasonal 
uptick in end-user demand has resulted in US physical 
premiums jumping to multi-year highs. In China, end-user 
output of white goods remains strong, while construction and 
autos demand is still growing but at a slower pace. This is 
helping to sustain strong growth in galvanised steel output, 
though we understand that growth in supply has been 
outpacing spot demand, and this could pose a downside risk 
to galvaniser’s zinc demand growth over the summer months.
